summary: Proposes a Mail Box Protocol, a standard way for a site to receive sequential files for immediate or deferred printing or other uses. A sending program would send the file with optional control codes. It does not decide how the site stores or prints the file. It was replaced by RFC 221.

eli5.summary: A drop box outside every computer where you can leave a file, and the owner prints it later. The note says how to drop it in.

subtitle: A network drop box for files to be printed or processed.

tldr.problem: Early network sites needed a standard, simple way to send documents to remote computers for printing or further processing without having to know each site's file system commands and naming conventions.
tldr.mechanism: The Mail Box Protocol defines numbered mail boxes at each site, where a sending program deposits sequential files (messages or documents) formatted as 7-bit ASCII with optional control codes. The receiving site handles storage, printing, or redistribution as appropriate for that site.
tldr.outcome: The protocol enabled simple document exchange, though it was soon replaced by more sophisticated file transfer and messaging protocols that provided better control and error handling.

today: RFC 221 (also called Mail Box Protocol) revised this approach. The Mail Box Protocol itself was supplanted by more sophisticated mail and file transfer mechanisms like SMTP, which provided better control over message delivery and error handling.

sections.title: Mail Boxes for Network Document Delivery
sections.content:
RFC 196 proposes a Mail Box Protocol as a standard mechanism for remote sites to send sequential files to each other. Each site maintains one or more numbered mail boxes (up to 128 per site). Senders deposit files into a mail box, and the receiving site handles them according to that site's policy—typically printing them, storing them for later retrieval, or redistributing them.

The protocol was motivated by the Network Information Center's (NIC) need to deliver documents to remote sites and to receive documents for cataloging and redistribution. Rather than requiring the NIC to know each site's unique file system and naming conventions, the mail box protocol provides a standard interface.
sections.eli5: Instead of learning how to use each computer's file system, you just drop a file in its mailbox, and it handles it from there.

sections.title: Format and Control Codes
sections.content:
Mail boxes use a simple format: messages are strings of 8-bit bytes, normally 7-bit ASCII with the high bit zero. The standard mail box (number 0) assumes a printer with a 72-character line and 66-line page, using carriage return and line feed (CR LF) for newlines and form feed (FF) to move to a new page.

Senders can use optional control codes to specify the mail box number, transmission code type (ASCII, transparent 8-bit, or EBCDIC), and printer settings such as line width and page size. At the head of a message to mail box 0, an address string identifies the sender and receiver, formatted for a clerk to read and distribute by hand.
sections.eli5: You format your file like a normal text document, optionally add instructions about how to print it, then send it. The receiving computer figures out the rest.

sections.title: Network Layering and Simplicity
sections.content:
The Mail Box Protocol builds on established network conventions: the Network Control Program (NCP), the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP), and the Data Transfer Protocol. A sender initiates a connection to a standard socket (candidate: socket 5) and follows the Modes Available handshake before transmitting control information and data.

The protocol's strength is its simplicity. It delegates the details of file handling, storage, and printing to each site, avoiding the complexity of specifying how every host should organize its files or what file systems it uses. This makes it practical across the diverse computers of the early ARPA Network.
sections.eli5: It uses the standard network setup (NCP, ICP, Data Transfer), then just sends your file with a few hints about formatting. Simple and it works.
